title: Lawful excuse
label: DPP v Ziegler · 2021
summary: The Supreme Court held that blocking a road in protest can be lawful if prosecution would be disproportionate. Within eighteen months, the courts confined it.
rule: It is an offence to wilfully obstruct a highway "without lawful authority or excuse" (Highways Act 1980, section 137). In *DPP v Ziegler* (2021) the Supreme Court held that when protest rights under Articles 10 and 11 are engaged, whether there was a lawful excuse can turn on whether a conviction would be proportionate. It restored the acquittals of protesters who had blocked a road.
nuance: *Ziegler* was widely read as making proportionality a defence to any protest offence. The Supreme Court later said that reading was mistaken.
In *DPP v Cuciurean* (March 2022) the Divisional Court held that a conviction for aggravated trespass is proportionate in itself, with no separate assessment needed.

In the Colston statue reference (September 2022) the Court of Appeal held that violent protest, or protest causing significant damage to property, falls outside Convention protection altogether. Proportionality is then not a question for the jury.
*Ziegler* still matters where an offence includes a lawful-excuse element and the protest is peaceful, as with obstructing a highway.
why_it_matters: Whether proportionality is a live question decides whether a jury or magistrate weighs the protester's rights at all.

history.text: *DPP v Ziegler*: the Supreme Court restores the protesters' acquittals.
*DPP v Cuciurean*: no separate proportionality assessment for aggravated trespass.
Colston statue reference: violent conduct or significant damage falls outside Convention protection.
Northern Ireland safe access zones reference: the Supreme Court says the wide reading of *Ziegler* was mistaken.
